Book Review
CyberpunkDystopian

Neuromancer

by William Gibson
★★★☆☆

Neuromancer's worldbuilding is nothing short of pioneering, essentially inventing cyberpunk with ideas that still feel unsettlingly prescient today, but the story itself grows convoluted and hard to follow after a stunning opening. Flat dialogue and unnecessary sexual content hold it back further, though its genre-defining influence remains undeniable

William Gibson·November 2025

I am a huge fan of the cyberpunk genre. There is something about the rainy, dark, neon filled dystopia where corporations rule everything and small resistance stories unfold in the shadows that has always intrigued me. Maybe it is because our own world is slowly moving toward a reality that resembles it. I often read short stories in this genre, play video games built around the cyberpunk aesthetic and spend a lot of time watching videos about how the genre came to be. In almost every source I came across, people repeated the same claim. William Gibson, a science fiction classic, is the starting point of it all. He is considered the pioneer of cyberpunk.

Moreover, one of my long term goals is to write my own cyberpunk story set in a futuristic version of Turkey, more specifically Istanbul. I always felt that the city, with its crowded streets and chaotic energy, is the perfect home for a dystopian future. So reading this science fiction classic felt necessary if I want to achieve that goal and understand how the genre began. Neuromancer is not just an important book. It is the foundation of almost everything I love about cyberpunk.

I was, however, disappointed. I will explain why as the review continues, but I want to be clear that my disappointment had nothing to do with the worldbuilding or the ideas that shaped the genre. Those parts were impressive and it is easy to see why Neuromancer became so influential. My issue was with the story itself.

The book actually opened in an incredible way. My favorite line in the entire novel appears in the very first sentence:

“The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.”

That single sentence set the tone perfectly. It created an atmosphere that was cold, empty and futuristic in a way only cyberpunk can achieve. When I read it, I thought to myself that I was about to read a masterpiece. The opening chapters supported that feeling. The exposition was sharp and immersive, and it immediately made me believe in the bleak, futuristic dystopia Gibson was building.

But after those first chapters, the story became very convoluted. It started to jump around in ways that were hard to follow. The plot lost its clarity and the momentum that the opening chapters established slowly faded. Sometimes the exposition itself stood in the way of the narrative, making everything heavier and more confusing. I found myself re reading certain passages just to understand what was happening, and that constant effort pulled me out of the experience.

One thing I can say without hesitation is that Neuromancer was far ahead of everyone else in terms of worldbuilding. It does not just create a genre that reshaped science fiction. It also predicts the future in ways that are genuinely unsettling. Reading it today feels strange because so many of the ideas Gibson wrote about in the early eighties are now part of our everyday reality. It is eye opening and impressive. Using real world company names like Sony also grounds the setting and strengthens immersion.

I would like to pause for a moment and talk about the genre defining impact of this book. Cyberpunk 2077 is one of my favorite games and one of the works that made me fall in love with the cyberpunk aesthetic. Before that I was mostly into fantasy. After reading Neuromancer, it became obvious how many concepts, terms and technologies that appear in the game were inspired by Gibson’s work. Seeing ideas from a book published in 1984 left me shocked. Neuromancer is not just an important science fiction novel. It is one of the pillars of the entire genre.

Despite this influence, the story itself did not live up to my expectations. The dialogue often felt flat and abrupt. I never truly connected with the conversations between characters. The book is also surprisingly short. I honestly think the story could have benefited from being longer and more detailed. Maybe if Gibson had expanded certain parts, the plot would not have felt so chaotic. A little more space for the story to breathe might have fixed many of the problems I had with it.

I have no issue with adult themes in fiction, especially in cyberpunk. They come naturally with the atmosphere. However, they still need to serve a purpose. The violent and gory moments in Neuromancer made sense and fit the tone. The sexual scenes, on the other hand, felt unnecessary and did nothing for the plot. They did not build character or advance the story. They were simply there for the sake of being there.

Another thing we need to acknowledge is how different the reading experience is today compared to the eighties. For a modern reader, many of Gibson’s ideas do not feel new because we already live with similar technologies and social structures. But for someone reading this in 1984, these concepts would have been mind blowing. The book would have expanded the imagination of its original audience in a way that is difficult for us to feel today. This historical context is important when evaluating the novel.

There were things I enjoyed despite my frustrations. I liked that the crew travels across different parts of the world. Each location has its own culture shaped by religion, politics and environment. Seeing how different societies evolved within this cyberpunk future added depth to the setting. Still, one thing annoyed me. It takes a special effort to travel all the way to Istanbul and somehow not include even one Turkish character. It felt like a missed opportunity in a city that could have added so much character to the narrative.

The book is also hard to follow and the language is dense. If this is your first introduction to science fiction, I recommend reading a few easier works before diving into Neuromancer. It can be overwhelming because of the technical terms and the abstract writing style. Even though I was disappointed with the story, I was completely satisfied with the worldbuilding. Neuromancer is a pioneering work of science fiction that created a genre which remains strong today and continues to inspire countless creators.

We should never forget that cyberpunk exists because of William Gibson. His influence is undeniable and his vision shaped an entire movement. My final rating for this book is 3 out of 5 stars.

By Ruşen M. Özoruç
